title: Beatles Songs
subtitle: Nine songs from easy to hard, plus a toolbox for working songs out by ear
description: Learn from Beatles songs, ordered by difficulty. Every song teaches one thing: a chord trick, a moving line, a scale or a playing technique, tied back to the chord and scale lessons. You learn the chords and techniques here, then play along with the recording.

lessons.title: Love Me Do: two chords, one hand shape
lessons.summary: The first Beatles single. Switch between I and IV without moving your hand.

steps.title: How this course works
steps.body:
Every lesson is one Beatles song, from easy to hard, and every song teaches one new thing: a chord trick, a line, a technique.

There are no lyrics or sheet music here. You learn the **chords and the technique** in the app, then you **listen to the recording and play along**. That's how the Beatles learned songs too: from records, by ear.

**Tip:** most music players and video sites let you slow a song down (playback speed 0.75). Start slow, the key stays the same.

steps.title: Why Love Me Do
steps.body:
Their first single (1962) is in **G major** and the verse uses just two chords: **G (I)** and **C (IV)**. The middle section adds **D (V)**. It's the I–IV–V family from the chord course.

The lesson here is a hand-shape trick. G is **G B D**. If you play C as **G C E** instead of C E G, the **G stays under your thumb** and only two fingers move. That's the second inversion, written **C/G**. Smooth changes come from keeping shared notes still.

steps.prompt: Play C with G as the lowest note (G C E).
steps.explain: G C E. The thumb stays on G, the note C shares with G.

steps.prompt: Verse: switch G, C/G, G, C/G. Keep your thumb on G the whole time.
steps.explain: Only fingers 3 and 5 move up one step. That's why it feels effortless.

steps.title: The middle section: V – IV – I
steps.body:
The middle of the song climbs to **D (V)**, steps down to **C (IV)** and lands on **G (I)**. That's the I–V–IV rock turnaround from the chord course, just started from V.

Left hand: play the **root of each chord** low on the keys (G, C, D). Right hand: the chord on every beat.

steps.prompt: Middle section: V, IV, I.
steps.explain: D, C, G. Tension, step down, home.

steps.prompt: Left hand bass line: the roots of the whole song.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here. Then play it with the recording: one bass note per bar, right hand chords on every beat.
steps.explain: G and C a fourth apart, then D, C, G. Your left hand just found its first bass line.

steps.question: In G major, which chord is IV?
steps.explain: Count G A B C: the fourth note is C, so IV is C major.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Put the recording on and play **left hand roots + right hand chords on every beat**. Listen for where the song changes from G to C. The harmonica riff and the middle section will tell you when D comes.

**Practice goal:** play the whole song once along with the record without stopping. Mistakes are fine, stopping is not: if you lose your place, just wait for the next G.

lessons.title: Let It Be: the pop progression on piano
lessons.summary: I–V–vi–IV with a steady right hand and a walking fill in the bass.

steps.title: Why Let It Be
steps.body:
Paul plays this one on piano, in **C major**, white keys only. It's built from the **I–V–vi–IV** pop progression you already know, and its little cousin **I–V–IV–I**.

The piano part is the lesson: a **steady right hand** playing chords in even pulses, and a left hand that holds the bass.

steps.prompt: First half of the verse: I, V, vi, IV.
steps.explain: C, G, Am, F. The pop axis.

steps.prompt: Second half: I, V, IV, I.
steps.explain: Ends at home, ready to start again.

steps.prompt: Chorus: vi, V, IV, I. It starts on the minor chord.
steps.explain: Am, G, F, C. Starting on vi makes the chorus feel more serious, then it walks down home.

steps.title: The piano pattern
steps.body:
**Left hand:** the root of each chord, held for the whole bar (two bars per chord feel is also fine).

**Right hand:** the chord, played in **even pulses**: start with 4 per bar, later 8. Keep the hand close to the keys and let the wrist do the bouncing.

**The fill:** at the end of the chorus the bass walks down **F – E – D – C** under the chords **F – C/E – Dm – C**. It's an inversion trick: C with E in the bass fills the gap between F and Dm.

steps.prompt: Left hand: the walking fill, F E D C.
steps.practice: 5 rounds, slow and even. Then play it under the chords below.
steps.explain: Four steps down to home. Listen for it at the end of the chorus.

steps.prompt: The fill with chords: IV, I⁶ (C with E in the bass), ii, I.
steps.explain: The bass walks F, E, D, C while the chords follow.

steps.question: Which one is the first half of the verse?
steps.explain: Progression 1 has the minor vi (Am). Progression 2 is the second half, I–V–IV–I.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
With the recording: left hand roots, right hand chords in 4 even pulses per bar. When that's easy, go to 8.

**Practice goal:** 3 times through along with the record. Then try it **without** the record, singing the melody in your head, and add the walking fill at the end of each chorus.

lessons.title: Hey Jude: V7, I7 and the long ♭VII outro
lessons.summary: A piano ballad in F with three tricks, and four minutes to improvise over.

steps.title: Why Hey Jude
steps.body:
Another Paul piano song, in **F major** (one flat: B♭, from the F scale lesson). It shows three tricks:

**1. V7:** C7 pulls hard back to F.
**2. I7:** add E♭ to F and it becomes F7, which pulls to **B♭ (IV)**. A chord can point to a new chord, not only home.
**3. ♭VII:** the long outro repeats **F – E♭ – B♭ – F** (I–♭VII–IV–I) for about four minutes.

steps.prompt: The verse: I, V, V7, I, IV, I, V7, I.
steps.explain: F, C, C7, F, B♭, F, C7, F. Hear how C7 leans harder towards F than plain C.

steps.title: I7: the door to IV
steps.body:
F7 is **F A C E♭**. That E♭ is not in F major, and it wants to fall to D, a note of B♭. So F7 works like the **V7 of B♭**.

The middle section of the song uses exactly this move: F7 opens the door and the song steps into B♭.

steps.prompt: Play I, I7, IV.
steps.explain: F, F7, B♭. The E♭ drops to D. One note turned home into a signpost.

steps.title: The outro: I–♭VII–IV–I
steps.body:
E♭ is **♭VII**, borrowed from F minor (the color-chord lesson). E♭ to B♭ to F: each chord is a fourth below the last, a very open, anthem-like sound.

Because it repeats for minutes, the outro is the best place in any Beatles song to **improvise**. The scale that fits all three chords is F major with E♭ instead of E: **F G A B♭ C D E♭**. That's called **F Mixolydian**.

steps.prompt: Outro: I, ♭VII, IV, I.
steps.explain: F, E♭, B♭, F.

steps.prompt: Right hand: F Mixolydian, the outro scale, up and down.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here, 5 daily. Note finger 4 on B♭, the same as the F major scale.
steps.explain: F major with an E♭. Every note fits the outro.

steps.question: Which chord does F7 want to move to?
steps.explain: F7 is the V7 of B♭. Its E♭ falls to D and its A rises to B♭.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Play the verse along with the recording, left hand roots, right hand chords. Then skip to the outro: left hand plays F, E♭, B♭, F, and your **right hand improvises with F Mixolydian**. Start with slow single notes, land on F or C at the end of each round.

**Practice goal:** improvise over the whole outro once without stopping.

lessons.title: I Want to Hold Your Hand: III7 and a visit to IV
lessons.summary: A major chord where you expect minor, and a ii–V–I in a new key.

steps.title: Why this song
steps.body:
A fast, joyful early single in **G major**. Two lessons:

**1.** The verse goes **G – D – Em – B7**. In G major the chord on B should be **Bm**, but they play **B7**: **B D♯ F♯ A**. That D♯ is outside the key and pulls up to E. B7 is the **V7 of Em**, a *secondary dominant*.

**2.** The middle section plays **Dm7 – G7 – C**: a **ii–V–I in C**. For a moment C (IV) feels like home.

steps.prompt: Play B7, the III7 in G.
steps.explain: B D♯ F♯ A. The D♯ is the leading tone of Em.

steps.prompt: Verse: I, V, vi, III7, then back to I.
steps.explain: G, D, Em, B7, G. B7 sets up Em, but the song goes back to G instead: a nice surprise.

steps.prompt: End of the verse: IV, V, I, vi, IV, V, I.
steps.explain: C, D, G, Em, C, D, G. Plain I–IV–V, the bright payoff.

steps.title: The middle section: a ii–V–I in C
steps.body:
The bridge plays **Dm7 – G7 – C – Am**, twice. In the key of C that's **ii7 – V7 – I – vi**, the ii–V–I from the chord course. Then it builds back with **C – D** over and over (IV–V in G) until the verse returns.

This is how songs **change key for a moment**: play the ii–V of the new key and the ear follows.

steps.prompt: Bridge, thinking in C: ii7, V7, I, vi, ii7, V7, I.
steps.explain: Dm7, G7, C, Am. Same chords as the ii–V–I lesson.

steps.prompt: Right hand: B7 broken up, then landing on Em. Feel D♯ rise to E.
steps.practice: 5 rounds. Play it slowly and listen to the D♯ → E pull.
steps.explain: D♯ is the note that makes B7 point to Em.

steps.question: In C major, which chord would be the V7 of Am (vi)?
steps.explain: Five notes up from A is E, so the V7 of Am is E7: III7 in C.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
This one is fast. Slow the recording down first. Right hand: chords on **every beat**, short and punchy, like the hand claps. Left hand: roots.

**Practice goal:** play the verse and middle section along with the slowed-down recording, then at full speed.

lessons.title: Yesterday: a detour into the minor chord
lessons.summary: A ii–V into the minor vi, a bass line that walks down, and ballad broken chords.

steps.title: Why Yesterday
steps.body:
On the record it's Paul's guitar and a string quartet, sounding in **F major**. On piano it becomes a ballad lesson.

Right after the first chord the song takes a detour: **Em7 – A7 – Dm**. A7 has a C♯, outside the key: it's the **V7 of Dm**, written **III7** in F. And Em7 is the ii of Dm. So Em7 – A7 – Dm is a little **ii–V–i into the relative minor**, Dm (vi).

Then the bass **walks down D – C – B♭** into **B♭ (IV)**, and **C7 (V7)** brings it home.

examples.label: F – Em7 – A7 – Dm – B♭ – C7 – F

steps.prompt: Play F, Em7, A7, Dm.
steps.explain: F, Em7, A7, Dm. The C♯ in A7 pulls up to D.

steps.prompt: Now the way home: vi, vi7 with C in the bass, IV, V7, I.
steps.explain: Dm, Dm7/C, B♭, C7, F. The bass walks D, C, B♭.

steps.prompt: Left hand: the bass line of the whole phrase.
steps.practice: 5 rounds. Use the fingers that feel natural; many ballad players take every low bass note with finger 5 or 4.
steps.explain: F, E, A, D, then down C, B♭, and C7 to F.

steps.title: Ballad broken chords
steps.body:
Instead of hitting chords, a ballad often plays them **one note at a time**: 1–3–5–3 of the chord, over the bass note. It keeps the sound moving while the tempo is slow.

Keep the hand in one shape per chord and move the whole shape. Fingers **1, 3, 5, 3**.

steps.prompt: Right hand: broken chords F, Dm, B♭, C7, F.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here, then daily with the left hand bass under it.
steps.explain: Each chord keeps the same hand shape. B♭ is played as D F B♭ so the hand barely moves.

steps.question: In F major, which chord leads strongly into Dm?
steps.explain: A is five notes above D, so A7 is the V7 of Dm. Its C♯ pulls to D.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Play along softly: left hand bass notes, right hand broken chords. When the music gets to the detour (Em7 – A7 – Dm), listen to how the A7 makes the Dm sound inevitable.

**Practice goal:** one full, slow, even play-through with the record.

lessons.title: In My Life: IV to iv, and a solo built from scales
lessons.summary: The borrowed minor iv, and fast clean scale runs.

steps.title: Why In My Life
steps.body:
In **A major** (three sharps: F♯, C♯, G♯). The verse is **A – E – F♯m – A7 – D – Dm – A**: I–V–vi–I7–IV–**iv**–I.

Two tricks you know: **A7** points to D (like F7 in Hey Jude), and **D → Dm** is the borrowed minor iv from the color-chord lesson. One note changes, **F♯ drops to F**, and the line keeps falling to E in the A chord. That's the bittersweet sigh.

steps.prompt: The verse: I, V, vi, I7, IV, iv, I.
steps.explain: A, E, F♯m, A7, D, Dm, A. Listen to the D → Dm moment.

steps.prompt: Both hands: the falling line F♯ – F – E over the bass D, D, A.
steps.practice: 5 rounds. Play it slowly, the second note a little softer.
steps.explain: That half-step line is the whole emotional effect of IV–iv–I.

steps.title: The solo
steps.body:
The solo is a fast baroque-style piano piece. George Martin played it at **half speed, an octave lower**, then the tape was sped up. That's why it sounds like a harpsichord and is so fast.

You don't need it note for note to learn from it: it's made of **A major scale runs**. The way to get fast and clean is the repetition rule: **slow and even first**, then 4 to 6 bpm faster when 3 rounds in a row are clean.

steps.prompt: Right hand: A major scale, one octave up and down.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here, 5 daily. Start at 60 bpm, two notes per click when that's clean.
steps.explain: The thumb goes under after C♯ on the way up and finger 3 crosses over to C♯ on the way down.

steps.prompt: Left hand: A major scale.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here, 5 daily plus 2 extra for the left hand.
steps.explain: Finger 3 crosses over to F♯ going up; the thumb goes under to E going down.

steps.question: In A major, which note changes when IV (D) becomes iv (Dm)?
steps.explain: D major is D F♯ A. D minor is D F A. Only the third drops.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Play the verse with the record: left hand roots, right hand chords. Make the D → Dm change obvious by holding the chord a bit longer.

At the solo, play **A major scale runs** in time with the record, up and down. **Practice goal:** stay in time through the whole solo, even if you only play quarter notes.

lessons.title: Something: chords with a line moving inside
lessons.summary: C – Cmaj7 – C7 – F: one voice falls chromatically while the chord stays.

steps.title: Why Something
steps.body:
George Harrison's ballad, in **C major**. Its signature is a **chromatic line inside the chords**: the chord stays C, but one note slides down **C – B – B♭ – A**:

**C** (C E G) → **Cmaj7** (B on top) → **C7** (B♭ on top) → **F** (A on top).

This is called a **line cliché**. It turns a static chord into a little melody.

steps.prompt: Play I, Imaj7, I7, IV.
steps.explain: C, Cmaj7, C7, F. C7 is also the I7 → IV move from Hey Jude.

steps.prompt: Both hands: the line C – B – B♭ – A on top, C and F in the bass.
steps.practice: 5 rounds. Then fill in the chords with your middle fingers.
steps.explain: The left hand holds C while the right hand slides down, then both land on F.

steps.title: The same trick in minor
steps.body:
Next the song goes **D7 → G**: **II7 – V**, the V7 *of* V (a secondary dominant again: F♯ pulls to G).

Then the line cliché comes back on **Am**: the top note falls **A – G♯ – G – F♯** (Am, Am with G♯, Am7, D7). And the phrase ends with **F – E♭ – G – C**: IV – **♭III** – V – I. E♭ is borrowed from C minor. It's the same E♭ chord as in Hey Jude, but in C it sits on the third step, so it's ♭III.

steps.prompt: Play II7, V.
steps.explain: D7, G. F♯ rises to G.

steps.prompt: Both hands: the minor line A – G♯ – G – F♯ over A, then D in the bass.
steps.explain: Same idea in minor: one voice slides down a half step at a time.

steps.prompt: End of the phrase: IV, ♭III, V, I.
steps.explain: F, E♭, G, C. The E♭ is a surprise before the normal V–I.

steps.question: What moves when C becomes Cmaj7 in this song?
steps.explain: The chord stays C; only the top note slides down a half step. That's a line cliché.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Play along with the record at a slow tempo. Right hand plays the chords **with the moving note on top** so you hear the line clearly. Left hand: roots, or a held C under the whole line cliché.

**Practice goal:** play the verse along with the recording, making both lines (C B B♭ A and A G♯ G F♯) audible.

lessons.title: Eleanor Rigby: minor, Dorian and staccato
lessons.summary: Two chords, a minor mode with a raised sixth, and short sharp playing.

steps.title: Why Eleanor Rigby
steps.body:
No Beatle plays an instrument on this one: it's a **string octet** (arranged by George Martin) playing short, driving chords. It's in **E minor** and mostly uses just two chords: **Em (i)** and **C (VI)**.

The melody has a twist: sometimes it uses **C♯** instead of C. Minor with a raised sixth is called **Dorian**. It sounds less sad and more like an old folk song.

steps.prompt: Play VI, i (C, then Em).
steps.explain: C to Em: the opening move.

steps.prompt: Right hand: E natural minor, up and down.
steps.explain: E F♯ G A B C D: the same notes as G major, starting on E.

steps.prompt: Right hand: E Dorian. Same scale with C♯ instead of C.
steps.practice: 3 rounds here, then alternate the two scales daily.
steps.explain: One note different, and the whole mood shifts.

steps.question: Which one is Dorian?
steps.explain: Melody 2 has C♯, the raised sixth. Melody 1 has C, natural minor.

steps.title: The chorus line: E – D – C♯ – C
steps.body: The chorus moves **Em – Em7 – Em6 – C**. Look at the top: **E – D – C♯ – C**. It's the line cliché from Something, in minor. And Em6 contains the C♯: the Dorian sixth again.

steps.prompt: Both hands: the line E – D – C♯ – C over the bass E, then C.
steps.explain: One voice slides down while the bass holds E, then the bass drops to C.

steps.title: Staccato: short and sharp
steps.body:
The strings play **staccato**: every chord short, with silence in between. On piano: drop onto the keys from just above them and **bounce off with the wrist**, not the arm. Fingers stay firm, wrist stays loose.

Start with 4 short chords per bar, all equally loud.

steps.prompt: Play i, VI, i as short staccato chords (4 bounces each when you practise on your own).
steps.explain: Em, C, Em. Short, sharp, even.

steps.question: What makes Dorian different from natural minor?
steps.explain: Dorian = natural minor with the 6th raised a half step. In E: C becomes C♯.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
With the recording: left hand E (or C) as a low bass note, right hand **staccato chords** on every beat. In the chorus, play the falling line E D C♯ C on top.

**Practice goal:** keep the staccato even through the whole song, without the chords getting longer when you get tired.

lessons.title: Lady Madonna: boogie left hand and ♭VI–♭VII–I
lessons.summary: A rolling left hand, independent hands, and a borrowed climb to home.

steps.title: Why Lady Madonna
steps.body:
Paul's rocking piano song in **A major**, inspired by 1950s boogie-woogie and rhythm-and-blues piano. Two lessons:

**1. Harmony:** the verse rocks between **A (I)** and **D (IV)**, then climbs **F – G – A**: **♭VI – ♭VII – I**. F and G are borrowed from A minor, and climbing through them makes A sound like a big arrival.

**2. Technique:** a **left hand that keeps moving** while the right hand plays something different. That's real hand independence, the hardest skill in this course.

steps.prompt: Play the verse shape: I, IV three times, then ♭VI, ♭VII, I.
steps.explain: A, D, A, D, A, D, F, G, A.

steps.title: A boogie bass pattern
steps.body:
Here's a classic boogie pattern (a general pattern, not the record's exact riff): **root – fifth – sixth – fifth**, over and over, in a bouncy swing rhythm. On A: **A – E – F♯ – E**. On D: **D – A – B – A**.

Fingers **5 – 2 – 1 – 2**. The hand shape stays the same; just move it to the next root.

steps.prompt: Left hand: the boogie pattern on A, twice, then on D, twice.
steps.practice: 5 rounds plus 2 extra. When it's even, swing it: long-short, long-short.
steps.explain: Root, fifth, sixth, fifth. Same shape on every chord.

steps.prompt: Left hand: the same pattern on F, G and A for the climb home.
steps.explain: F and G use the same shape. Only the A pattern has a black key.

steps.title: Hands together
steps.body:
Now add the right hand: a short **A chord on beats 2 and 4** (the off beats) while the left hand keeps the pattern going. Start with just one right hand note, **C♯**, so your brain only has to manage the rhythm.

Practise at **60 bpm** first. If the left hand stops when the right hand plays, slow down further.

steps.prompt: Both hands: left hand boogie on A, right hand C♯ on the 2nd and 4th notes.
steps.practice: 5 rounds. Then replace the C♯ with a full A chord (A C♯ E), and later move both hands to D.
steps.explain: Right hand on the off beats, left hand never stops. That's the boogie feel.

steps.question: In A major, which chords are ♭VI and ♭VII?
steps.explain: Lower the 6th and 7th degrees of A major (F♯, G♯) and build major chords: F and G.

steps.title: Now play along with the record
steps.body:
Play along with a slowed-down recording. First only the left hand pattern, following A and D, and the F – G – A climb. Then add short right hand chords on the off beats.

**Practice goal:** one full verse hands together without the left hand stopping. Tempo comes later.

lessons.title: Your Beatles toolbox: work songs out by ear
lessons.summary: Hear the tricks from this course, then find the chords of new songs yourself.

steps.title: How to work out a song
steps.body:
**1. Find home.** Hum the end of the chorus and find that note: that's the key.
**2. Find the bass.** Play along with single bass notes. Bass notes are the roots of most chords.
**3. Try I, IV, V and vi first.** They cover most of any song.
**4. Something sounds outside the key?** Check your Beatles toolbox:

**♭VII** (Hey Jude) · **♭III** (Something) · **iv** after IV (In My Life) · **III7** right before the vi chord (I Want to Hold Your Hand, Yesterday) · **I7** before IV (Hey Jude) · **♭VI–♭VII–I** (Lady Madonna) · a **moving inner line** (Something, Eleanor Rigby).

steps.question: Which progression has the In My Life trick?
steps.explain: Progression 1 goes IV → iv: the major chord turns minor before home.

steps.question: Which one uses the borrowed ♭VII?
steps.explain: Progression 2: C, B♭, F, C. The Hey Jude outro shape.

steps.question: Which one has a secondary dominant pulling into the minor chord?
steps.explain: Progression 2 turns Em into E7, the V7 of Am: the G♯ pulls up to A. Same trick as B7 in I Want to Hold Your Hand and A7 in Yesterday.

steps.question: Which ending climbs home through borrowed chords?
steps.explain: A♭, B♭, C: ♭VI–♭VII–I, the Lady Madonna climb.

steps.question: Which one has a line moving inside the chord?
steps.explain: Progression 1 is the Something line cliché: C, B, B♭, A on top.

steps.title: Songs to try on your own
steps.body:
Use the steps above with the recording, and look for these tricks:

**Here Comes the Sun:** the middle section repeats **♭VII – IV – I**.
**With a Little Help from My Friends:** the chorus uses **♭VII – IV – I** too.
**While My Guitar Gently Weeps:** a minor key with a **bass line walking down** under the chords.
**Michelle:** a **chromatic line** falling inside a minor chord.

Write down the chords you find, then play them along with the record. If a chord sounds wrong, check the bass note first.

steps.question: A chord sounds outside the key, and right after it the song lands on the vi chord. What should you try first?
steps.explain: A secondary dominant: in C that's E7 before Am. You heard it in I Want to Hold Your Hand and Yesterday.
